vignette:
Minh has always found comfort in the order of things. As a tax inspector, his world is one of ledgers, codes, and regulations-a universe where every number has its place and every discrepancy can, with enough patience, be reconciled. For twenty-five years, this logic has been his shield. His life with his wife, Lien, is built on a similar foundation of quiet predictability: dinners at six, gardening on Saturdays, the soft murmur of the television in the evenings. It is a world he carefully constructed, a fortress against the chaos he never speaks of.

The chaos has a name: Eliza. He met her twelve years ago, during a brief separation from Lien. Eliza was vibrant, exciting, a whirlwind of passion that felt like a new beginning after years of comfortable quiet. At first, her intensity was intoxicating. But soon, the passion began to curdle. Her moods would swing with a terrifying velocity, a cheerful morning dissolving into a storm of accusations by lunch. He remembers the first time she threw a plate. It shattered against the wall behind him, and the shock was so profound he couldn't move. He, a man who had never even raised his voice, stood frozen as she screamed at him for some imagined slight.

The violence escalated from there, always followed by tearful apologies and promises it would never happen again. He learned to read the subtle shifts in her tone, the tightening of her jaw, the way her eyes would go flat just before an eruption. He became an expert in de-escalation, abandoning his own opinions, his own needs, to keep the peace. The physical abuse was sporadic but brutal-a shove that sent him stumbling into a bookshelf, a slap that left his ear ringing for days, once a punch to the ribs that made it hard to breathe for a week. He hid the bruises under his crisp work shirts. The shame was a heavier weight than any injury. He was a man, a respected professional. Who could he tell? What would they think? The narrative didn't fit. So he buried it, auditing his own memories and redacting the parts that didn't align with the man he was supposed to be.

It took him nearly two years to leave. He finally broke it off after she threatened him with a kitchen knife during an argument over a burnt dinner. He packed a bag while she was at work and never went back, eventually reconciling with Lien, who asked few questions and simply welcomed him home.

For a time, he thought he had successfully filed the experience away, a closed case in a locked drawer. But the past refuses to stay balanced. Now, a decade later, the interest is coming due. He finds himself re-reading the same line of a tax return a dozen times, his focus shattered. The sharp, sudden laughter of a female colleague in the next cubicle makes his heart hammer against his ribs, his body tensing for a blow that never comes. He has become a stranger in his own home. When Lien reaches across the table for the soy sauce, his arm instinctively jerks back to shield his face. The hurt in her eyes is immediate, a fresh entry in the long ledger of his failings.

Sleep offers no refuge. He often wakes in a cold sweat, the ghost of Eliza's perfume in the air, his body rigid with a fear that has no present-day source. He feels perpetually on guard, scanning rooms, mapping exits, assessing threats that only he can see. He loves Lien, he knows this in an abstract, intellectual way, but the feeling itself is distant, muffled. Joy, contentment, peace-they are assets he can see on a balance sheet but cannot access for himself. He moves through the routines of his life, a man meticulously accounted for on the outside, but inside, he is running a deficit so profound he no longer knows how to calculate the loss.
